Appreciate the clear list — we can do that. I'm attaching a short PDF with the high-level answers (SIG_Acme_answers.pdf) and will follow up with the isolation playbook and network diagram by early next week.

High-level bullets here so you have something immediately:
- Dedicated GPU pools are generally allocated as tenant-bound node pools; customers get isolated node sets (no shared tenant processes).
- We enforce process & namespace isolation at the container level and restrict access to GPU devices via cgroup device whitelisting.
- For supported hardware (A100/MIG-capable instances) we use GPU partitioning (MIG) where requested; otherwise we schedule single-tenant workloads to avoid oversubscription.
- KV/prefix cache is namespaced per-tenant and encrypted at rest; we never share hot KV cache memory across tenant processes.
- Network boundaries are customer-configurable (VPC peering, private endpoints).

I'll route this to our SREs and ops team for the playbook and metric exports — cc'ing Vivek and Stephanie to pull artifacts.

Jonas / Steph — attaching my draft of the isolation playbook and a short technical note (I referenced in the note: isolation_playbook.docx and network_diagram.png). Highlights below for the customer email: 

- Pool model: Dedicated pools are allocated as tenant-bound Kubernetes node pools. We either reserve whole nodes for a single tenant, or on MIG-capable hardware we carve GPU partitions per-tenant. We avoid multi-tenant scheduling on non-MIG GPUs.
- Process isolation: containers run with strict Linux namespaces, seccomp, and cgroups; GPU device nodes are exposed selectively to containers using device plugins and cgroup device rules.
- KV cache & memory: cache namespaces are per-tenant. We run an LRU per-namespace and enforce an upper memory cap per tenant; on eviction we log and surface metrics. No shared in-process cache across tenants.
- Noisy neighbor detection: we emit GPU utilization, SM stall counters, kernel latency, per-tenant token latency p50/p95/p99, and KV hit/miss rates to our observability pipeline. We alert on delta of tenant latency/consumption vs baseline and trigger automated mitigation (cgroup throttling, migrate job to isolated node, or scale-out).
- Mitigation playbook: 1) detect via aggregated alerts, 2) instrument and collect process/GPU stacktrace, 3) if transient spike, throttle via cgroup or evict offending pod, 4) if persistent, migrate tenant to dedicated single-tenant node or enable MIG partitions, 5) post-incident remediation (quota adjustment, billing credit review if SLO breached).
- Evidence: we can export a week of metric series and an anonymized example incident timeline showing detection -> mitigation.

I'll attach the docx and a cleaned diagram for them to consume. If we want to include a short snippet of kube/node security config (taints/tolerations, device plugin config), I can paste it into the PDF.

Vivek
Principal SRE, Redwood Inference

Attachments (included in ZIP / attached individually):
- SIG_Acme_answers.pdf — concise SIG answers and references to the deeper artifacts.
- isolation_playbook.docx — SRE runbook for noisy-neighbor detection & mitigation (play-by-play and responsibilities).
- network_diagram.png — logical diagram showing tenant VPCs, private endpoints, and Dedicated pool placement.

Key points: 
- Dedicated pools are designed to provide strong isolation: either whole-node single-tenant allocation or hardware partitioning (MIG) when requested.
- We never co-locate unrelated tenant processes on the same OS process space; GPU device access is gated by the container runtime and device plugin.
- KV cache namespace and memory caps prevent cross-tenant cache contamination; we maintain per-tenant telemetry for cache hit/miss and can export the metrics for audit.
- Our automated mitigation ladder is documented in the playbook; we can provide a redacted incident timeline as evidence.
